rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine pronoun may return to silver in 9:34 because it is more prevalent, and to trade in 62:11 because it is more important.
rows.anchor: فرد الكناية إلى الفضة لأنها الأغلب والأعم، وإلى التجارة لأنها الأفضل والأهم.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view makes the pronoun refer to prayer because patience is included in it, as the Messenger's approval is included in God's approval.
rows.anchor: إن الصبر لما كان داخلا في الصلاة أعاد عليها كما قال

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view refers it to both patience and prayer but omits the dual ending for brevity, as in the verse about Mary and her son and the cited poetry.
rows.anchor: رد الكناية إلى كل واحد منهما لكن حذف اختصارا قال الله تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The pronoun may refer to worship, which patience and prayer encompass in meaning.
rows.anchor: على العبادة التي يتضمنها بالمعنى ذكر الصبر والصلاة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: It may refer to the verbal noun seeking help, implied by the command to seek help.
rows.anchor: على المصدر، وهي الاستعانة التي يقتضيها قوله: { واستعينوا }

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: It may refer to Muhammad's response, since patience and prayer were among the matters he called people to.
rows.anchor: على إجابة محمد عليه السلام لأن الصبر والصلاة مما كان يدعو إليه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: It may refer to the Kaaba, since prayer is commanded toward it.
rows.anchor: على الكعبة لأن الأمر بالصلاة إنما هو إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kabīrah means heavy and difficult and is the predicate of inna; a non-Qur'anic form could use the masculine pronoun.
rows.anchor: { وكبيرة } معناه ثقيلة شاقة، خبر «إن». ويجوز في غير القرآن: وإنه لكبيرة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer is light for the humble; the masters of spiritual meanings say they are people supported from eternity by election and guidance.
rows.anchor: { إلا على الخاشعين } فإنها خفيفة عليهم. قال أرباب المعاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khashiʿūn means humble people; khushūʿ is an inward state that appears in the limbs as stillness and humility.
rows.anchor: الخاشعون جمع خاشع وهو المتواضع. والخشوع: هيئة في النفس يظهر منها في الجوارح سكون وتواضع.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah locates khushūʿ in the heart as fear, with lowering the gaze during prayer as its outward sign.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: الخشوع في القلب، وهو الخوف وغض البصر في الصلاة.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the humble person visibly shows abasement, like a house made desolate after its inhabitants leave.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: الخاشع الذي يرى أثر الذل والخشوع عليه كخشوع الدار بعد الإقواء.

rows.speaker: النابغة
rows.claim: Al-Nābighah's line uses khāshiʿ for an old dwelling's worn, quiet appearance, illustrating the root's basic sense.
rows.anchor: قال النابغة: رماد ككحل العين لأيا أبينه ونؤي كجذم الحوض أثلم خاشع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root describes an obscure place and quiet voices; khashʿah is a soft piece of land, and a khāshiʿ town is dusty and uninhabited.
rows.anchor: ومكان خاشع: لا يهتدى له. وخشعت الأصوات أي سكنت.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other lexical senses are sticky sputum in the chest and lowering the gaze; a hadith calls a soft patch on water a khashʿah before it was spread out.
rows.anchor: وخشعت خراشي صدره إذا ألقى بصاقا لزجا. وخشع ببصره إذا غضه.

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash rebuked Sufyān for seeking leadership without understanding khushūʿ and rejected rough food, rough clothes, and a bowed head as its definition.
rows.anchor: سألت الأعمش عن الخشوع فقال: يا ثوري، أنت تريد أن تكون إماما للناس ولا تعرف الخشوع!

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī defines khushūʿ as treating noble and lowly alike in matters of right and humbling oneself to God in every duty.
rows.anchor: لكن الخشوع أن ترى الشريف والدنيء في الحق سواء، وتخشع لله في كل فرض افترض عليك.

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: ʿUmar told a youth who had lowered his head to raise it, since outward posture cannot add to what is in the heart.
rows.anchor: يا هذا! ارفع رأسك، فإن الخشوع لا يزيد على ما في القلب.

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: ʿAlī says khushūʿ is in the heart, includes gentleness toward a Muslim, and means not turning during prayer.
rows.anchor: الخشوع في القلب، وأن تلين كفيك للمرء المسلم، وألا تلتفت في صلاتك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says the fuller treatment will come with the description of believers who are humble in prayer.
rows.anchor: وسيأتي هذا المعنى مجودا عند قوله تعالى: قد أفلح المؤمنون الذين هم في صلاتهم خاشعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Displaying more humility to people than exists in the heart is hypocrisy added to hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: فمن أظهر للناس خشوعا فوق ما في قلبه فإنما أظهر نفاقا على نفاق.

rows.speaker: سهل بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Sahl says none is truly humble until every hair is humbled, citing the verse about believers' skins shivering.
rows.anchor: قال سهل بن عبد الله: لا يكون خاشعا حتى تخشع كل شعرة على جسده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī calls heart-born fear the praised khushūʿ: it compels unfeigned outward composure and submission; the early generations tried to conceal its visible signs.
rows.anchor: هذا هو الخشوع المحمود لأن الخوف إذا سكن القلب أوجب خشوع الظاهر فلا يملك صاحبه دفعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feigning humility through affected tears or a bowed head to win esteem is blameworthy deception from Satan and self-delusion.
rows.anchor: وأما المذموم فتكلفه والتباكي ومطأطأة الرأس كما يفعله الجهال ليروا بعين البر والإجلال

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reports that ʿUmar jabbed or punched a man who sighed theatrically as if pretending to grieve.
rows.anchor: روى الحسن أن رجلا تنفس عند عمر بن الخطاب كأنه يتحازن فلكزه عمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī describes ʿUmar as audible when speaking, quick when walking, forceful when striking, a genuine ascetic and truly humble man.
rows.anchor: وكان عمر رضي الله عنه إذا تكلم أسمع، وإذا مشى أسرع، وإذا ضرب أوجع

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid, transmitted by Ibn Abī Najīḥ, says the humble are the true believers.
rows.anchor: وروى ابن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد قال: الخاشعون هم المؤمنون حقا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request occurred during the wandering, after they tired of manna and quail and remembered their former life in Egypt.
rows.anchor: كان هذا القول منهم في التيه حين ملوا المن والسلوى، وتذكروا عيشهم الأول بمصر.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says they were people accustomed to leeks, onions, and lentils, and their appetites returned to their bad old habits.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: كانوا نتانى أهل كراث وأبصال وأعداس، فنزعوا إلى عكرهم عكر السوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They called manna and quail one food though they were two because they ate one together with the other.
rows.anchor: وكنوا عن المن والسلوى بطعام واحد وهما اثنان لأنهم يأكلون أحدهما بالآخر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says the two foods repeated daily, so they were called one regular fare, like a person constant in one practice.
rows.anchor: لتكرارهما في كل يوم غذاء كما تقول لمن يداوم على الصوم والصلاة والقراءة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that they could not bear universal prosperity, which left no one needing help; the passage says they were the first to use slaves and servants.
rows.anchor: لن نصبر على الغنى فيكون جميعنا أغنياء فلا يقدر بعضنا على الاستعانة ببعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭaʿām can mean anything eaten or drunk; Qur'anic 'taste' can include drinking wine, and honey as salwā would also be a drink.
rows.anchor: الطعام يطلق على ما يطعم ويشرب قال الله تعالى: ومن لم يطعمه فإنه مني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Food can conventionally mean grain or dates specifically; Abū Saʿīd's report on zakāt al-fiṭr contrasts a measure of food with barley.
rows.anchor: صاعا من طعام أو صاعا من شعير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary usage, a food market means the place where food is sold, not every place selling something edible or drinkable.
rows.anchor: والعرف جار بأن القائل: ذهبت إلى سوق الطعام، فليس يفهم منه إلا موضع بيعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥah, ṭaʿm can mean what taste conveys or something desirable; with ḍammah it means food.
rows.anchor: والطعم بالفتح: هو ما يؤديه الذوق يقال: طعمه مر. والطعم أيضا: ما يشتهى منه

rows.speaker: أبو خراش
rows.claim: Abū Khirāsh's poetry uses ṭaʿm first for food and then for its savor or desirability.
rows.anchor: قال أبو خراش: أرد شجاع البطن لو تعلمينه وأوثر غيري من عيالك بالطعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb ṭaʿima means to eat or taste; it means 'taste' in 2:249 and 'eat' in 33:53.
rows.anchor: وقد طعم يطعم فهو طاعم إذا أكل وذاق ومنه قوله تعالى: «ومن لم يطعمه فإنه مني»

rows.speaker: النبي محمد
rows.claim: The Prophet described Zamzam as nourishment for the hungry and a cure for illness.
rows.anchor: وقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في زمزم: «إنها طعام طعم وشفاء سقم»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asking someone to feed one a report means asking them to tell it; an imam's being asked to be fed means prompting him when he loses his recitation.
rows.anchor: يقول: إذا استفتح فافتحوا عليه. وفلان ما يطعم النوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unnamed poet describes ostriches at Wajrah as tasting sleep only while fasting, illustrating the idiom.
rows.anchor: وقال الشاعر: نعاما بوجرة صفر الخدو د ما تطعم النوم إلا صياما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Banū ʿĀmir pronounce fa-dʿu with kasrah on ʿayn at the consonant meeting, treating the defective verb like a sound verb.
rows.anchor: لغة بني عامر «فادع» بكسر العين لالتقاء الساكنين يجرون المعتل مجرى الصحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yukh'rij is jussive as though the command says, 'Ask Him and say: bring forth'; al-Zajjāj weakens the alternative that supplies a deleted lām.
rows.anchor: و «يخرج» مجزوم على معنى سله وقل له: أخرج، يخرج.

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash regards min in mimmā as extra, while Sībawayh treats it as non-extra because the clause is affirmative.
rows.anchor: و «من»، في قوله «مما» زائدة في قول الأخفش، وغير زائدة في قول سيبويه لأن الكلام موجب.

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās says al-Akhfash sought an object for yukh'rij by treating mā as that object.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: وإنما دعا الأخفش إلى هذا لأنه لم يجد مفعولا ل «يخرج»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī prefers an omitted object inferred as edible food; the first min is partitive and the second specifies.
rows.anchor: والأولى أن يكون المفعول محذوفا دل عليه سائر الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min bāqlihā is an appositive for mā with the preposition repeated; qiththāʾ and the remaining foods are coordinated with it.
rows.anchor: بدل من «ما» بإعادة الحرف. { وقثآئها } عطف عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baql is any plant without a stem, while a tree has one; qiththāʾ is cucumber, and Yaḥyā b. Waththāb and Ṭalḥah read its qāf with ḍamma, a less common variant.
rows.anchor: والبقل معروف، وهو كل نبات ليس له ساق. والشجر: ما له ساق.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qithāʾ can form qithāʾī, is a wāw-root, and aqthaʾa can mean to feed people it.
rows.anchor: إلا أن قثاء من ذوات الواو تقول: أقثأت القوم أي أطعمتهم ذلك.

rows.speaker: الجعدي
rows.claim: Al-Jaʿdī's poetry uses nafthāʾ for calming a boiling pot by adding water, illustrating the root's sense of calming.
rows.anchor: قال الجعدي: تفور علينا قدرهم فنديمها ونفثؤها عنا إذا حميها غلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The f-th-ʾ root also means calming anger, tiring from running, or heat subsiding; the proverb says sour curdled milk calms anger.
rows.anchor: إن الرثيئة تفثأ في الغضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rathīʾah is milk curdled by milking it onto sour milk; irtathaʾa means the milk thickened.
rows.anchor: الرثيئة: اللبن المحلوب على الحامض ليخثر.

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: ʿĀʾishah says her mother succeeded in fattening her for introduction to the Prophet only after feeding her cucumber with fresh dates; al-Qurṭubī grades the chain sound.
rows.anchor: عن عائشة قالت: «كانت أمي تعالجني للسمنة، تريد أن تدخلني على رسول الله

rows.speaker: جويبر عن الضحاك
rows.claim: Juwaybir reports from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that fūm means garlic because it pairs with onion; this view invokes interchange of fāʾ and thāʾ.
rows.anchor: فقيل: هو الثوم، لأنه المشاكل للبصل. رواه جويبر عن الضحاك.

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reads thūmihā with thāʾ; the same reading is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود «ثومها» بالثاء المثلثة وروي ذلك عن ابن عباس.

rows.speaker: أمية بن أبي الصلت
rows.claim: Umayyah b. Abī al-Ṣalt's line listing gardens and al-fūm supports interpreting fūm as garlic.
rows.anchor: كانت منازلهم إذ ذاك ظاهرة فيها الفراديس والفومان والبصل

rows.speaker: حسان
rows.claim: Ḥassān pairs fūm with onion as food, supporting the garlic view adopted by al-Kisāʾī and al-Naḍr b. Shumayl.
rows.anchor: وقال حسان: وأنتم أناس لئام الأصول طعامكم الفوم والحوقل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and most exegetes identify fūm as wheat; al-Naḥḥās prefers this view because its support is stronger and its chains sound.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الفوم الحنطة روي عن ابن عباس أيضا وأكثر المفسرين واختاره النحاس

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās rejects the garlic view despite al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ: interchange cannot be extended by analogy and is uncommon in Arabic.
rows.anchor: والإبدال لا يقاس عليه وليس ذلك بكثير في كلام العرب.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās answered a questioner who said fūm means wheat by citing a line of Uḥayḥah b. al-Jallāḥ about wheat cultivation.
rows.anchor: وأنشد ابن عباس لمن سأله عن الفوم وأنه الحنطة، قول أحيحة بن الجلاح

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj argues that the people would not request food without grain, the foundation of nourishment.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق الزجاج: وكيف يطلب القوم طعاما لا بر فيه، والبر أصل الغذاء!

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawharī defines fūm as wheat and al-Akhfash cites a supporting wheat-cultivation poem.
rows.anchor: وقال الجوهري أبو نصر: الفوم الحنطة. وأنشد الأخفش

rows.speaker: ابن دريد
rows.claim: Ibn Durayd says fūmah means an ear of wheat and cites a line describing ears in a scout's hand.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن دريد: الفومة السنبلة وأنشد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other dialectal explanations make fūm chickpeas in Syrian speech; fāmī is an altered nisbah of fūmī, and fūmū lanā means bake for us.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: الفوم: الحمص لغة شامية. وبائعه فامي، مغير عن فومي

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ calls fūmū lanā an old dialect for 'bake for us'; ʿAṭāʾ and Qatādah define fūm as any grain made into bread.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: هي لغة قديمة. وقال عطاء وقتادة: الفوم كل حب يختبز.

rows.speaker: جمهور العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars permit eating onions, garlic, and other foul-smelling greens because sound reports establish their permissibility.
rows.anchor: فذهب جمهور العلماء إلى إباحة ذلك للأحاديث الثابتة في ذلك.

rows.speaker: طائفة من أهل الظاهر
rows.claim: Some literalists who hold congregational prayer obligatory prohibit these foods, arguing that deliberately doing what prevents an obligation is forbidden and the Prophet called them foul.
rows.anchor: وذهبت طائفة من أهل الظاهر القائلين بوجوب الصلاة في الجماعة فرضا إلى المنع

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Jābir reports that the Prophet told a companion to eat greens after finding them in a pot, explaining that he privately converses with one the companion does not; Muslim and Abū Dāwūd transmit it.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أتي ببدر فيه خضرات من بقول فوجد لها ريحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī takes Jābir's report to show the restriction was particular to the Prophet, while others may eat these foods.
rows.anchor: أخرجه مسلم وأبو داود. فهذا بين في الخصوص له والإباحة لغيره.

rows.speaker: أبو أيوب
rows.claim: Abū Ayyūb served the Prophet food with garlic; asked whether it was forbidden, the Prophet said no, but that he disliked it. Muslim records the report.
rows.anchor: فقال: أحرام هو؟ قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «لا ولكني أكرهه»

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abū Saʿīd reports the Prophet saying at Khaybar that he does not prohibit what God made lawful but dislikes the smell of garlic.
rows.anchor: أيها الناس إنه ليس لي تحريم ما أحل الله ولكنها شجرة أكره ريحها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These reports suggest a personal restriction because the Prophet alone was singled out for conversation with the angel.
rows.anchor: فهذه الأحاديث تشعر بأن الحكم خاص به، إذ هو المخصوص بمناجاة الملك.

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Jābir's report establishes the shared rule: anyone eating garlic, onion, or leek must not approach the mosque because angels are harmed by what harms people.
rows.anchor: فلا يقربن مسجدنا فإن الملائكة تتأذى مما يتأذى منه بنو آدم

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: In a report transmitted by Muslim, ʿUmar says the Prophet removed people smelling of onion or garlic from the mosque to al-Baqīʿ and ordered eaters to cook them thoroughly.
rows.anchor: إذا وجد ريحهما من الرجل في المسجد أمر به فأخرج إلى البقيع، فمن أكلهما فليمتهما طبخا

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: A report attributed to ʿAlī from the Prophet calls lentils blessed and sanctified, softening the heart and increasing tears, and says seventy prophets including Jesus blessed them.
rows.anchor: عليكم بالعدس فإنه مبارك مقدس وإنه يرق القلب ويكثر الدمعة

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz alternated bread with oil, meat, and lentils on successive days.
rows.anchor: وكان عمر بن عبد العزيز يأكل يوما خبزا بزيت، ويوما بلحم، ويوما بعدس.

rows.speaker: الحليمي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥalīmī calls lentils and olive oil food of the righteous; their connection with Abraham's hospitality is itself a virtue, and lentils ease worship without stirring desire like meat.
rows.anchor: قال الحليمي: والعدس والزيت طعام الصالحين ولو لم يكن له فضيلة إلا أنه ضيافة إبراهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wheat is the soundest identification of fūm, barley was close and fed Medina, and lentils were food in Abraham's town, linking the grains to the two prophets.
rows.anchor: والحنطة من جملة الحبوب وهي الفوم على الصحيح، والشعير قريب منها وكان طعام أهل المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet and his household never ate their fill of wheat bread for three consecutive days from his arrival in Medina until his death.
rows.anchor: لم يشبع هو وأهله من خبز بر ثلاثة أيام متتابعة منذ قدم المدينة إلى أن توفاه الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istibdāl means putting one thing in place of another, as with badal.
rows.anchor: الاستبدال: وضع الشيء موضع الآخر ومنه البدل، وقد تقدم.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj derives adnā from d-n-w, closeness in value: a comparable garment is cheap.
rows.anchor: مأخوذ عند الزجاج من الدنو أي القرب في القيمة

rows.speaker: علي بن سليمان
rows.claim: ʿAlī b. Sulaymān derives adnā from the base dāniʾ, low or vile, with the hamzah softened.
rows.anchor: هو مهموز من الدنيء البين الدناءة بمعنى الأخس، إلا أنه خفف همزته.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another derivation takes adnā from dūn, inferior: its form began as adwan, underwent metathesis, and changed final wāw to alif.
rows.anchor: هو مأخوذ من الدون أي الأحط فأصله أدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A noncanonical reading is adnaʾ, with hamzah.
rows.anchor: وقرىء في الشواذ «أدنأ».

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse asks whether they exchange inferior herbs, cucumbers, grain, lentils, and onions for the better manna and quail.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الآية: أتستبدلون البقل والقثاء والفوم والعدس والبصل الذي هو أدنى

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: First, al-Zajjāj says manna and quail are better because the requested vegetables have little worth by comparison.
rows.anchor: الأول: أن البقول لما كانت لا خطر لها بالنسبة إلى المن والسلوى كانا أفضل قاله الزجاج.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Second, God's gift came with a command to eat it, so continuing in obedience and gratitude brought afterlife reward, unlike their request.
rows.anchor: في استدامة أمر الله وشكر نعمته أجر وذخر في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Third, what God gave them was more delicious than what they requested.
rows.anchor: لما كان ما من الله به عليهم أطيب وألذ من الذي سألوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fourth, God's food came without effort, while their requested food required cultivation, agriculture, and toil.
rows.anchor: والذي طلبوه لا يجيء إلا بالحرث والزراعة والتعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fifth, manna and quail were certainly lawful as gifts from God, whereas dealings in crops could involve usurpation and doubt.
rows.anchor: لما كان ما ينزل عليهم لا مرية في حله وخلوصه لنزوله من عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse permits eating wholesome, pleasurable foods; the Prophet liked sweets and honey and drank cool, fresh water.
rows.anchor: في هذه الآية دليل على جواز أكل الطيبات والمطاعم المستلذات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to go down to a town was a challenge incapacitating them, as in the command to become stone or iron.
rows.anchor: وهذا أمر معناه التعجيز كقوله تعالى: قل كونوا حجارة أو حديدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their being commanded to descend while in the wandering was a punishment.
rows.anchor: لأنهم كانوا في التيه وهذا عقوبة لهم.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative report says they were given the food they asked for.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنهم أعطوا ما طلبوه.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and others take tanwīn miṣran as an indefinite town among the towns.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد وغيره: فمن صرفها أراد مصرا من الأمصار غير معين.

rows.speaker: عكرمة عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿIkrimah transmits Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: a town among these towns.
rows.anchor: وروى عكرمة عن ابن عباس في قوله: «اهبطوا مصرا» قال: مصرا من هذه الأمصار.

rows.speaker: طائفة ممن صرفها
rows.claim: Other grammarians who read the word with tanwīn still identify it as Egypt itself.
rows.anchor: وقالت طائفة ممن صرفها أيضا: أراد مصر فرعون بعينها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite-town view cites the apparent order to enter a town and reports that they lived in Syria after the wandering; the Egypt view cites their inheritance of Pharaoh's lands.
rows.anchor: استدل الأولون بما اقتضاه ظاهر القرآن من أمرهم دخول القرية

rows.speaker: الأخفش والكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and al-Kisāʾī permit tanwīn because the name is light like Hind and Daʿd, citing a poem that uses both case forms.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش والكسائي: لخفتها وشبهها بهند ودعد وأنشد

rows.speaker: سيبويه والخليل والفراء
rows.claim: Sībawayh, al-Khalīl, and al-Farrāʾ reject that declension, reasoning that Zayd would not take tanwīn as a woman's name.
rows.anchor: وسيبويه والخليل والفراء لا يجيزون هذا لأنك لو سميت امرأة بزيد لم تصرف.

rows.speaker: غير الأخفش
rows.claim: Another grammarian explains the tanwīn by saying the word means a place, making it declinable.
rows.anchor: وقال غير الأخفش: أراد المكان فصرف.

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبان بن تغلب وطلحة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Abān b. Taghlib, and Ṭalḥah read Miṣr without tanwīn; the Ubayy codex and Ibn Masʿūd likewise identify Pharaoh's Egypt.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وأبان بن تغلب وطلحة: «مصر» بترك الصرف.

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik told Ashhab that this is Egypt, his own town and Pharaoh's residence, as quoted by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah.
rows.anchor: قال أشهب قال لي مالك: هي عندي مصر قريتك مسكن فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miṣr originally means boundary; miṣr al-dār is the house's limit, and Ibn Fāris says people of Hajar used the term for property boundaries.
rows.anchor: والمصر أصله في اللغة الحد. ومصر الدار: حدودها.

rows.speaker: عدي
rows.claim: ʿAdī's line calls the sun a clear boundary dividing day from night, illustrating the root meaning.
rows.anchor: قال عدي: وجاعل الشمس مصرا لا خفاء به بين النهار وبين الليل قد فصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā is the object governed by inna in 'you have what you asked for.'
rows.anchor: «ما» نصب بإن.

rows.speaker: ابن وثاب والنخعي
rows.claim: Ibn Waththāb and al-Nakhaʿī read saʾaltum with kasrah on sīn; saʾalta and salta are both used, and yatasāwalan shows the wāw root.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن وثاب والنخعي «سألتم» بكسر السين يقال: سألت وسلت بغير همز.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍuribat ʿalayhim means humiliation and poverty were imposed and decreed, an image compared to pitching tents; the verb can mean a judge imposed a penalty.
rows.anchor: أي ألزموهما وقضي عليهم بهما مأخوذ من ضرب القباب

rows.speaker: الفرزدق
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq's line to Jarīr uses ḍuribat for an affliction imposed and sealed by scripture.
rows.anchor: قال الفرزدق في جرير: ضربت عليك العنكبوت بنسجها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī glosses dhillah as abasement and maskanah as poverty, claiming that even a rich Jew displays poverty's dress, submission, and humiliation.
rows.anchor: والذلة: الذل والصغار. والمسكنة: الفقر.

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah explain dhillah as the obligation of paying jizyah.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الذلة فرض الجزية عن الحسن وقتادة.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj takes maskanah as submissiveness, deriving it from stillness because poverty reduces movement.
rows.anchor: والمسكنة الخضوع، وهي مأخوذة من السكون أي قلل الفقر حركته قاله الزجاج.

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbaydah glosses dhillah as lowliness; maskanah is the verbal noun of miskīn.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: الذلة الصغار. والمسكنة مصدر المسكين.

rows.speaker: الضحاك بن مزاحم عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk transmits Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation of the people struck by humiliation and poverty as holders of tax-farming contracts.
rows.anchor: وروى الضحاك بن مزاحم عن ابن عباس: { وضربت عليهم الذلة والمسكنة }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bāʾū means they returned and remained bound to the consequence; the root means return, including the prayer acknowledging and binding oneself to God's blessing.
rows.anchor: { وبآءوا } أي انقلبوا ورجعوا أي لزمهم ذلك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bawāʾ can mean returning retribution for blood or equal status in a matter, as poetry also describes return with captives and spoils.
rows.anchor: والبواء: الرجوع بالقود. وهم في هذا الأمر بواء أي سواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says the meaning of divine anger has already been treated in the Fātiḥah.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم معنى الغضب في الفاتحة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhālika explains the cause: they disbelieved in God's book and prophets' miracles, including those of Jesus, John, Zechariah, and Muhammad, and killed prophets.
rows.anchor: { بأنهم كانوا يكفرون } أي يكذبون { بآيات الله } أي بكتابه ومعجزات أنبيائه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan has a variant reading of yaqtulūn; another transmission from him matches the common reading.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الحسن «يقتلون» وعنه أيضا كالجماعة.

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ reads al-nabiyyīn with hamzah throughout the Qur'an except two verses in al-Aḥzāb, where he leaves it unlengthened and unhamzated; the other readers omit hamzah throughout.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع «النبيئين» بالهمز حيث وقع في القرآن إلا في موضعين: في سورة الأحزاب:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two exceptions to Nāfiʿ's hamzated reading are 33:50 and 33:53, where he reads without lengthening or hamzah because two kasrah hamzahs meet; other readers omit hamzah everywhere.
rows.anchor: إن وهبت نفسها للنبي إن أراد [الأحزاب: 50]. لا تدخلوا بيوت النبي إلا [الأحزاب: 53]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamzated form derives from anbaʾa, 'inform': nabīʾ is an active participle, plural anbiyāʾ, with nabāʾ also attested as a plural.
rows.anchor: فأما من همز فهو عنده من أنبأ إذا أخبر واسم فاعله منبىء.

rows.speaker: العباس بن مرداس
rows.claim: Al-ʿAbbās b. Mirdās's praise of the Prophet as the seal of nabāʾ supports the hamzated form.
rows.anchor: قال العباس بن مرداس السلمي يمدح النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: يا خاتم النبآء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those omitting hamzah either derive the word from the same root with a softened hamzah or from nabā yanbū, 'to rise'; nabwah is elevation.
rows.anchor: فمنهم من اشتق اشتقاق من همز، ثم سهل الهمز. ومنهم من قال: هو مشتق من نبا ينبو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without hamzah, nabī can mean a path; a messenger is called nabī because people are guided by him as by a road.
rows.anchor: والنبي بترك الهمز أيضا الطريق، فسمي الرسول نبيا لاهتداء الخلق به كالطريق

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: An unnamed poet uses nabī for a path on the ground, supporting the unhamzated lexical sense.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر: لأصبح رتما دقاق الحصى مكان النبي من الكاثب

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: A report where the Prophet rejects nabīʾ with hamzah and accepts nabī without it has a weak chain, according to Abū ʿAlī; the Prophet's uncorrected hearing of a hamzated poem also weakens it.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: ضعف سند هذا الحديث ومما يقوي ضعفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Without right' magnifies the enormity of the killing; it does not imply any prophet could deserve execution, since none did an act requiring it.
rows.anchor: فكان هذا تعظيما للشنعة عليهم ومعلوم أنه لا يقتل نبي بحق، ولكن يقتل على الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's allowing disbelievers to kill prophets honors them and raises their rank, as with believers slain in God's cause; it is not abandonment.
rows.anchor: ذلك كرامة لهم وزيادة في منازلهم كمثل من يقتل في سبيل الله من المؤمنين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan say prophets not commanded to fight could be killed, while every prophet commanded to fight was victorious.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والحسن: لم يقتل نبي قط من الأنبياء إلا من لم يؤمر بقتال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second dhālika points back to and reinforces the first; bi in bimā marks cause, and al-Akhfash glosses it as 'because of their disobedience.'
rows.anchor: «ذلك» رد على الأول وتأكيد للإشارة إليه. والباء في «بما» باء السبب.

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash interprets bimā as 'because of their disobedience'; disobedience opposes obedience, while transgression exceeds limits, especially in injustice and sins.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش: أي بعصيانهم. والعصيان: خلاف الطاعة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God foretells objections to turning believers from Syria toward the Kaaba; the future 'will say' is used like past speech to show the objection persists.
rows.anchor: أعلم الله تعالى أنهم سيقولون في تحويل المؤمنين من الشام إلى الكعبة: ما ولاهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Among people' is specified because foolishness may also be attributed to inanimate things and animals; the fools are all who ask why Muslims were redirected.
rows.anchor: وخص بقوله: «من الناس» لأن السفه يكون في جمادات وحيوانات.

rows.speaker: المؤرج
rows.claim: Al-Muʾarrij defines safīh as a slanderous liar who deliberately contradicts what he knows.
rows.anchor: وقال المؤرج: السفيه البهات الكذاب المتعمد خلاف ما يعلم.

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Quṭrub defines safīh as extremely unjust and ignorant.
rows.anchor: قطرب: الظلوم الجهول.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the fools as the Jews of Medina.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالسفهاء هنا اليهود الذين بالمدينة قاله مجاهد.

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī identifies them as the hypocrites.
rows.anchor: السدي: المنافقون.

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj identifies them as Quraysh, who said Muhammad longed for his birthplace and would soon return to their religion; Jews alleged he was confused, while hypocrites mocked the change.
rows.anchor: الزجاج: كفار قريش لما أنكروا تحويل القبلة قالوا: قد اشتاق محمد إلى مولده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wallāhum means that God turned or redirected them from their former direction.
rows.anchor: و «ولاهم» يعني عدلهم وصرفهم.

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports that people praying dawn at Qubāʾ were told the Prophet had been ordered to face the Kaaba, so they turned from Syria toward it; Mālik transmits this wording.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عمر قال: بينما الناس بقباء في صلاة الصبح إذ جاءهم آت فقال

rows.speaker: البراء
rows.claim: Al-Barāʾ reports in al-Bukhārī that the Prophet faced Jerusalem for sixteen or seventeen months, wished to face the House, and a worshipper told another mosque during prayer; they turned toward the Kaaba while bowing.
rows.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم صلى إلى بيت المقدس ستة عشر شهرا أو سبعة عشر شهرا

rows.speaker: البراء
rows.claim: Al-Barāʾ adds that people who died before the qiblah changed left uncertainty about their status, and the report then introduces a Qur'anic revelation.
rows.anchor: وكان الذي مات على القبلة قبل أن تحول قبل البيت رجال قتلوا لم ندر ما نقول فيهم
